full_judgment:
10. Learned Advocate Mr Md Abdul Baten Sheikh has appeared on behalf of the applicant-petitioner. [While Mr Sheikh, referring to the objection taken in the application, first of all submits that, the award dated 25-5-2017 is prima-facie contrary to the provisions of law in force in Bangladesh. In other words, the learned Advocate asserts that, receiving an advance rent or security deposit from the tenant, as consideration for the tenancy, is prohibited by section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991 (PRCA). However, if any such sum is paid to the landlord, in contravention of the provisions of section 10 of the PRCA, then the said amount is refundable as per provisions of section 14 of the PRCA. He argues that, an application should have been made, as per section 14 of the PRCA, to the Controller, within 6(six) months from the date of making such payment and the Controller may pass an order to refund or to make adjustment of the amount thus paid as advance or security. Therefore, he continues that, the amount claimed by the lessee was barred by special limitation prescribed in section 14 of the PRCA and the arbitrators had no authority to pass an award to refund the security or advance rent already time barred. Hence, he argues that, the award is prima-facie contrary to the provisions of section 10 read with section 14 of the PRCA. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate has cited a decision reported in 1985 BLD (AD) 77, between Mosammat Rahima Khatun vs Abdur Rashid Bhuiyan and another. He next submits that, the lease agreement dated 18-9-2011 was for a period of 5 (five) years, therefore, the deed ought to have been registered, as required by section 107 of the Transfer of Properties Act, 1882. Besides, he next submits, this lease deed should have been registered as required by clause (d) of section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908, as well. Therefore, this deed was ineffective in the eye of law, he contends, and no award should have been passed, based on this agreement. He also submits that, since the lease agreement dated 18-9-2011 has been executed for unlawful consideration, within the meaning of section 23 of the Contract Act, 1872, therefore, the agreement dated 18-9-2011 was void ab-initio and the arbitration clause was not enforceable in law and it did not constitute a valid arbitration agreement between the parties. As such, invoking arbitration clause was not legally permissible in this case, hence this award is not lawful, he insists. He refers to the decision of Tata Power Company Limited vs Dynamic Construction (the judgment passed in Civil Appeal No. 268 of 2009 by the Appellate Division, Supreme Court of Bangladesh and prays that, therefore, the application may be allowed and the award may be set-aside. 

 25. As such, mere reading of section 14 of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991, makes it clear that, the Rent Controller may have all the trappings of a civil court, but the order passed by the Rent Controller is not a decree of a court and, therefore, clearly the proceeding commenced before it by filing an application under section 14 of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991, is not a suit. Hence, section 14 of the PRCA does not prescribe any special limitation by substituting the first schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908.
